episode_title: How a 19-year-old intern built the growth engine behind this $2B AI company | Hector Serrano
description_html:
Hector Serrano runs one of the most innovative and successful paid growth programs in Silicon Valley. As Head of Content at Wispr Flow, a leading AI voice-to-text tool, he built a roster of 50 creators who drive 500 to 600 paid user-generated content (UGC) ads every month. The creators are paid a cut of ad spend, and the best of them earn over $13,000 a month. It’s a playbook the best DTC brands have used for years, now adapted for SaaS. Hector joined Wispr Flow at 19, before the product had PMF, and over the past year, Wispr Flow has grown revenue 30x and raised at a $2 billion valuation.

We discuss:

1. Why paid UGC is one of the biggest untapped growth levers right now

2. The step-by-step playbook for building a successful paid-UGC program

3. Why the best marketers are “allergic to AI”

4. What makes a great modern marketing hire

5. Why YouTube is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS

summary.overview: Hector Serrano describes joining Whisperflow at 19 with no startup experience and eventually leading its paid UGC content program and founder-led organic channels. The conversation focuses on Whisperflow’s product-led growth foundation, its shift from view-based organic UGC to performance-based paid creator ads, hiring and developing young talent, and using human-led content rather than AI-generated creative to cut through noise.

takeaways.heading: Product comes first
takeaways.detail: Hector says Whisperflow’s growth began with product-market fit and product-led growth: the product started gaining users organically before paid, organic, and other channels added fuel. He says there is no growth hack if users do not find the product valuable.

takeaways.heading: Paid from early on
takeaways.detail: Hector believes paid can be tested early, within a company’s budget, because converting cold traffic into paying users provides a clear signal about messaging and product value. He says saturation can often be addressed through new positioning, messaging, and ICPs.

takeaways.heading: Organic UGC limits
takeaways.detail: Whisperflow’s earlier organic UGC program paid creators by CPM to post on alternate TikTok and Instagram accounts. It generated about 500 million views in two and a half months, but was eventually shut down because the views produced too few conversions and encouraged vanity-metric chasing.

takeaways.heading: Performance-based UGC
takeaways.detail: The current program uses creators’ videos as paid ads, with creators receiving a percentage of ad spend for SaaS or GMV for e-commerce. Whisperflow uses Tribe to manage the program and was running roughly 500–600 new ads per month, with about 50 creators in the group.

takeaways.heading: Smart retainers
takeaways.detail: To reduce creators’ downside while they learn the system, Whisperflow may guarantee a payment for hitting a video quota, then subtract commissions from that amount. Once creators’ commissions exceed the retainer, they keep the uncapped commission earnings; some creators make around $13,000 per month.

takeaways.heading: Give creators freedom
takeaways.detail: Hector rejects lengthy briefs that prescribe every hook, line, and shot. He believes creators make better work when they are trusted to experiment, and cited an ad showing a keyboard outside in the rain that became one of Whisperflow’s best performers.

takeaways.heading: Build the creator group
takeaways.detail: He recommends targeted, manual outreach through Instagram, including searches for relevant niches and referrals through creators’ networks. Whisperflow began with a few carefully chosen creators, built community through meetings, coaches, giveaways, and a planned retreat, and later added a $100 referral payment for creators who recommend accepted members.

takeaways.heading: Match creators to ICPs
takeaways.detail: UGC is not limited to young creators: Whisperflow uses engineers, lawyers, mothers, salespeople, agency owners, and others who resemble specific audiences. Hector says technical or expensive products may need credible, older, or more specialized users rather than generic college-age creators.

takeaways.heading: Hire young talent
takeaways.detail: Hector recommends looking for evidence of content creation and audience-building, roughly 10,000–15,000 followers, hard work, cultural fit, and character rather than elite credentials. He contrasts his 2.5 GPA and Division I sports background with Tobin’s 4.0 GPA and Waterloo education, arguing both became strong marketers through different paths.

takeaways.heading: Give people time
takeaways.detail: Hector says he took about a year to feel comfortable at Whisperflow and spent his first months experimenting. He advocates a sports-academy approach: find young talent, coach them, give them money and freedom to test ideas, and allow them to fail while learning.

takeaways.heading: Lean operating team
takeaways.detail: The paid program mainly requires a creator/content lead and a media buyer. Hector manages creator communication, concepts, and approvals, while Eric manages ad accounts, spend, and performance across platforms such as Meta, LinkedIn, and YouTube.

takeaways.heading: AI and creative quality
takeaways.detail: Hector is not opposed to internal automation, but says AI should not yet produce the final creative people see, especially video, design, and ads. With increasing AI-generated noise, he believes high-quality, purposeful, human-made work can stand out more than publishing at maximum volume.

takeaways.heading: Founder-led content
takeaways.detail: Founder content makes a company feel human and builds trust over time. Whisperflow frames its content as an ongoing series tied to its mission of reaching one billion daily active users, covering launches, the founder’s life, company culture, and setbacks rather than immediately selling.

takeaways.heading: YouTube compounds
takeaways.detail: For founder-led content, Hector considers the long-form YouTube team especially important because titles, thumbnails, pacing, storytelling, and payoff determine whether strong footage gets watched. He says YouTube videos have a longer half-life than short-form posts and can continue generating views and customers years later.

takeaways.heading: Start creating
takeaways.detail: His advice to aspiring creators is to stop looking for more advice and turn on the camera. Even experienced creators struggle with retakes and imperfect delivery; consistent practice and publishing matter more than waiting for polished execution.

quotes.text: There's really no hack besides having a good product and then adding more and more levers to pull from.
quotes.speaker: Hector Serrano

quotes.text: When you send a creator a 10 page guideline on how they need to shoot their content, what they need to talk about, you end up removing the creative aspect that creators have.
quotes.speaker: Hector Serrano

quotes.text: I think the best advice would be to stop looking for advice.
quotes.speaker: Hector Serrano

quotes.text: You can't always connect the dots looking forward, but you can always connect them looking backwards.
quotes.speaker: Hector Serrano

quotes.text: If you actually focus more on the quality and less on the quantity ... it gets so easy to cut through the noise.
quotes.speaker: Hector Serrano
